title: AI May Have Solved Math's Greatest Mystery
text:
Science

Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims to have discovered an AI-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis, a 166-year-old mathematical problem concerning the distribution of prime numbers. His proof includes 17 million lines of code that reportedly compile successfully, but its underlying explanation exceeds 250,000 pages and remains inaccessible to human understanding. Alpöge also released advances on challenges involving the Euler and Navier-Stokes equations describing the flow of fluids such as air and water.

title: Virtual Cells Could Transform Medicine
text:
The New York Times

Efforts to develop AI-powered virtual cells that simulate how human cells function and respond to changes could potentially transform drug development, personalized medicine, and aging research. Researchers are building models trained on vast biological datasets, hoping to predict cellular behavior and identify treatments. Early systems such as GeneFormer, trained on data from about 30 million cells, have suggested promising therapeutic targets. Significant obstacles remain, particularly insufficient data and the complexity of cellular biology.

title: Electronics Industry Faces Global Circuit Board Shortage
text:
Bloomberg

The global electronics industry faces a growing shortage of printed circuit boards (PCBs). In a new advisory, the Global Electronics Association warned demand exceeds supply throughout the supply chain. Constraints are expected to continue through at least the first half of 2027, with meaningful relief unlikely before mid-2028. Because most PCBs are manufactured in Asia, the U.S. and Europe, which produce approximately 3% and 1%–2% of global output, respectively, are particularly vulnerable.

title: What a Robot Olympiad Reveals About Latin America's Future
text:
The Economist

Uruguay’s annual robotics competition attracted about 8,500 students this year, with the number of teams taking part increasing about 20-fold since 2015. Similar events are expanding in Brazil and Mexico, encouraging young people to build robots, program drones, and develop computational skills. Uruguay’s state-funded Ceibal program, which organizes the competition, supplies schools with robotics kits, 3D printers, and remote instruction in AI, as well as arranging classes via video-link with remote instructors who teach computational thinking and AI.

title: Unblockable Message Sent Using Gravity
text:
University of Queensland (Australia)

Researchers at Australia’s University of Queensland transmitted the word “Gravity” through a brick wall by moving an elevator’s 1.8-tonne counterweight to encode binary information. A sensitive gravimeter in an adjacent bathroom detected tiny changes in the gravitational field and decoded the message, demonstrating gravity can carry information through ordinary barriers. However, the experimental system was extremely slow, transmitting just one bit per minute.

title: Does This Man Have a Right to Data from His Own Brain?
text:
The New York Times

J. Galen Buckwalter, a paralyzed man with implanted brain-computer interface chips, is challenging the California Institute of Technology’s refusal to give him access to his neural data. He wants to use the recordings for personal research, commercial applications, and music, but the university says participants relinquish ownership under its consent terms. The dispute highlights unclear U.S. rules governing brain-data rights, with institutions generally controlling research information.

text:

The report found accelerated construction schedules increased contractor fees and risk premiums. title: Google Researchers Demonstrate Quantum Contextuality
text:
Interesting Engineering

Google researchers demonstrated quantum contextuality using its Willow processor, achieving a 98.3% success rate in the magic square game, exceeding the classical limit of 88.89%. Contextuality describes how quantum measurement outcomes depend on which other compatible measurements are performed. Researchers found contextuality tests revealed subtle hardware errors that conventional benchmarks may miss. These tests could improve quantum processor evaluation, clarify the origins of quantum advantage, and help advance error-corrected computing.

From "Google Researchers Demonstrate Quantum Contextuality"

title: Dutch Resist U.S. Bid to Tighten Semiconductor Export Controls
text:
Politico Europe

The Netherlands is opposing the proposed U.S. MATCH Act, which would require allies to align restrictions on advanced chipmaking equipment exports to China with U.S. rules. Dutch officials argue the legislation violates national sovereignty by allowing Washington to impose controls on foreign companies, particularly ASML, the leading lithography equipment manufacturer. The bill could expand restrictions on ASML’s sales and servicing of equipment in China, an important market.

title: U.S. Catholic Bishops' AI Task Force Urges Regulation, Worker Protections
text:
Associated Press

U.S. Catholic bishops are calling for stronger safeguards on AI, following Pope Leo’s appeal for robust regulation to protect humanity. A new bishops’ task force led by San Jose Bishop Oscar Cantú is engaging technology executives and political leaders, advocating protections for human dignity, workers, and young people. The group plans to promote AI literacy and monitor employment impacts. The bishops also updated investment guidelines, discouraging investments in companies developing AI technologies that fail to safeguard human dignity.

title: Cqlib: A High-Performance Software Stack for Quantum Computing
text: This paper presents Cqlib, a high-performance software stack for quantum computing built around a unified quantum circuit model. Its native Rust core provides efficient implementations of circuit processing, quantum-state and operator computation, compilation, and optimization, while Python and C interfaces support algorithm development and system integration. Cqlib covers quantum program construction, simulation, analysis, compilation, device adaptation, and result processing under consistent program semantics. Through OpenQASM and the Quantum Control Instruction Set (QCIS), Cqlib supports program representation and hardware-oriented execution. Cqlib further provides backend interfaces for device execution, with Cqlib-Tianyan serving as one implementation for QCIS-compatible quantum hardware. Evaluations using parameterized compilation tasks from Benchpress and related tests show that Cqlib achieves good functional coverage, compilation correctness, and execution efficiency within the evaluated task scope. We develop Cqlib-Algorithm as a modular library of reusable operators and composable components for widely used quantum algorithms, including quantum search, phase estimation, and variational algorithms, with additional support for error mitigation. To complement these building blocks with domain-specific workflows, we further develop Cqlib-VQE, Cqlib-QAOA, and Cqlib-QML for application-level studies in quantum chemistry, combinatorial optimization, and quantum machine learning, respectively. Cqlib also integrates source-grounded Skills and MCP-based tools to support agent-assisted program generation, backend execution, and result-guided workflow refinement. Overall, Cqlib provides a unified and extensible software foundation that connects quantum algorithm development, simulation, compilation, and execution on QCIS-compatible quantum hardware.

title: Tierkreis: A Dataflow Framework for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Computing
text: We present Tierkreis, a higher-order dataflow graph program representation and runtime designed for compositional, quantum-classical hybrid algorithms. The design of the system is motivated by the remote nature of quantum computers, the need for hybrid algorithms to involve cloud and distributed computing, and the long-running nature of these algorithms. The graph-based representation reflects how designers reason about and visualise algorithms, and allows automatic parallelism and asynchronicity. A strong, static type system and higher-order semantics allow for high expressivity and compositionality in the program. The flexible runtime protocol enables third-party developers to add functionality using any language or environment. With Tierkreis, quantum software developers can easily build, visualise, verify, test, and debug complex hybrid workflows, and immediately deploy them to the cloud or a custom distributed environment.

title: Quantum Computing: Vision and Challenges
text: The recent development of quantum computing, which uses entanglement, superposition, and other quantum fundamental concepts, can provide substantial processing advantages over traditional computing. These quantum features help solve many complex problems that cannot be solved otherwise with conventional computing methods. These problems include modeling quantum mechanics, logistics, chemical-based advances, drug design, statistical science, sustainable energy, banking, reliable communication, and quantum chemical engineering. The last few years have witnessed remarkable progress in quantum software and algorithm creation and quantum hardware research, which has significantly advanced the prospect of realizing quantum computers. It would be helpful to have comprehensive literature research on this area to grasp the current status and find outstanding problems that require considerable attention from the research community working in the quantum computing industry. To better understand quantum computing, this paper examines the foundations and vision based on current research in this area. We discuss cutting-edge developments in quantum computer hardware advancement and subsequent advances in quantum cryptography, quantum software, and high-scalability quantum computers. Many potential challenges and exciting new trends for quantum technology research and development are highlighted in this paper for a broader debate.

title: Entangling Disciplines: Causality, Entropy and Time-Travel Paradoxes on a Quantum Computer
text: Merging disciplines has led to incredible learnings and breakthroughs throughout history, including the discovery of quantum computing: a cross between computation and quantum physics. In this paper, I will discuss how we can cross quantum computing with topics in fundamental physics. This leads to fruitful, interactive learning opportunities that fuse deep open physics problems with key insights about quantum information science. By outlining quantum circuit experiments that can be run on current and near-term quantum computers, I demonstrate how to help learners engage with principles in special relativity, general relativity and thermodynamics. In turn, these connections can advance their understanding of quantum computing. Learners can further explore the quantum computing activities in this paper via the Quantum Paradoxes content series of videos, blogs and code tutorials that I created with IBM Quantum.

title: Unifying communication paradigms in measurement-based delegated quantum computing
text: Delegated quantum computing (DQC) allows clients with low quantum capabilities to outsource computations to a server hosting a quantum computer. This process is often envisioned within the measurement-based quantum computing framework, as it naturally facilitates blindness of inputs and computation. Hence, the overall process of setting up and conducting the computation encompasses a sequence of three stages: preparing the qubits, entangling the qubits to obtain the resource state, and measuring the qubits to run the computation. There are two primary approaches to distributing these stages between the client and the server that impose different constraints on cryptographic techniques and experimental implementations. In the prepare-and-send setting, the client prepares the qubits and sends them to the server, while in the receive-and-measure setting, the client receives the qubits from the server and measures them. Although these settings have been extensively studied independently, their interrelation and whether setting-dependent theoretical constraints are inevitable remain unclear. By implementing the key components of most DQC protocols in the respective missing setting, we provide a method to build prospective protocols in both settings simultaneously and to translate existing protocols from one setting into the other.

title: Arbitrary Ground State Observables from Quantum Computed Moments
text: The determination of ground state properties of quantum systems is a fundamental problem in physics and chemistry, and is considered a key application of quantum computers. A common approach is to prepare a trial ground state on the quantum computer and measure observables such as energy, but this is often limited by hardware constraints that prevent an accurate description of the target ground state. The quantum computed moments (QCM) method has proven to be remarkably useful in estimating the ground state energy of a system by computing Hamiltonian moments with respect to a suboptimal or noisy trial state. In this paper, we extend the QCM method to estimate arbitrary ground state observables of quantum systems. We present preliminary results of using QCM to determine the ground state magnetisation and spin-spin correlations of the Heisenberg model in its various forms. Our findings validate the well-established advantage of QCM over existing methods in handling suboptimal trial states and noise, extend its applicability to the estimation of more general ground state properties, and demonstrate its practical potential for solving a wide range of problems on near-term quantum hardware.

title: Quantum computing online workshops and hackathon for Spanish speakers: A case study
text:
We discuss the challenges and findings of organizing an online event in Spanish, consisting of a series of introductory workshops leading up to a quantum hackathon for Latin America. 220 Spanish speakers were registered, 66% of whom self-identified as being at an introductory level of quantum computing. We gain a better picture of the impact of quantum computing in Latin America, and the importance of generating educational resources in Spanish about quantum computing. Additionally, we report results on surveying the participants by country; educational status; self-reported levels of quantum computing, linear algebra, and Python competency; and their areas of interest within quantum.
  This event was organized by Quantum Universal Education with the Centro de Investigación en Computación del Instituto Politécnico Nacional (CIC-IPN) as the host institution, in collaboration with a number of organizations and companies: IBM Quantum, Xanadu, Multiverse Computing, Quantum Universal Education, Quantum Hispano, QMexico, Haq.ai, Dive in Learning. This was part of a larger event, the Qiskit Fall Fest 2021, as one of several hackathons organized around the world in a similar span of time. In each Qiskit Fall Fest hackathon, participants were challenged to form teams of up to 5, to develop in 5 days a project using the IBM Qiskit framework.

title: Strengths and Weaknesses of Quantum Computing
text: Recently a great deal of attention has focused on quantum computation following a sequence of results suggesting that quantum computers are more powerful than classical probabilistic computers. Following Shor's result that factoring and the extraction of discrete logarithms are both solvable in quantum polynomial time, it is natural to ask whether all of NP can be efficiently solved in quantum polynomial time. In this paper, we address this question by proving that relative to an oracle chosen uniformly at random, with probability 1, the class NP cannot be solved on a quantum Turing machine in time $o(2^{n/2})$. We also show that relative to a permutation oracle chosen uniformly at random, with probability 1, the class $NP \cap coNP$ cannot be solved on a quantum Turing machine in time $o(2^{n/3})$. The former bound is tight since recent work of Grover shows how to accept the class NP relative to any oracle on a quantum computer in time $O(2^{n/2})$.

title: Quantum Computing in the NISQ era and beyond
text: Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) technology will be available in the near future. Quantum computers with 50-100 qubits may be able to perform tasks which surpass the capabilities of today's classical digital computers, but noise in quantum gates will limit the size of quantum circuits that can be executed reliably. NISQ devices will be useful tools for exploring many-body quantum physics, and may have other useful applications, but the 100-qubit quantum computer will not change the world right away --- we should regard it as a significant step toward the more powerful quantum technologies of the future. Quantum technologists should continue to strive for more accurate quantum gates and, eventually, fully fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Quantum computing and information extraction for a dynamical quantum system
text: We discuss the simulation of a complex dynamical system, the so-called quantum sawtooth map model, on a quantum computer. We show that a quantum computer can be used to efficiently extract relevant physical information for this model. It is possible to simulate the dynamical localization of classical chaos and extract the localization length of the system with quadratic speed up with respect to any known classical computation. We can also compute with algebraic speed up the diffusion coefficient and the diffusion exponent both in the regimes of Brownian and anomalous diffusion. Finally, we show that it is possible to extract the fidelity of the quantum motion, which measures the stability of the system under perturbations, with exponential speed up.
